reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in SUOX, encoding the molybdenum-dependent enzyme sulphite oxidase
The enzyme catalyses the final step of sulphur amino acid catabolism, converting sulphite to sulphate; its deficiency causes accumulation of neurotoxic sulphite and S-sulphocysteine
Unlike molybdenum cofactor deficiency, xanthine oxidase is unaffected, so plasma uric acid is normal, which is the key distinguishing feature
The severe neonatal form presents with intractable seizures, feeding difficulty, hypotonia evolving to spasticity and rapidly progressive encephalopathy
Ectopia lentis (dislocation of the ocular lens) is a characteristic later finding
A fresh-urine sulphite dipstick may be positive, and raised urinary S-sulphocysteine supports the diagnosis; plasma total homocysteine is often low
Milder, later-onset phenotypes exist with developmental delay, movement disorder and a more indolent course
There is no established disease-modifying treatment, and dietary restriction of sulphur amino acids has limited proven benefit
reference.pathophysiology: Sulphite oxidase is a mitochondrial molybdoenzyme that oxidises sulphite to sulphate, the terminal reaction in the degradation of the sulphur-containing amino acids cysteine and methionine. When SUOX is defective, sulphite accumulates and reacts with cystine to form S-sulphocysteine, a structural analogue of glutamate that is thought to act as an excitotoxin at NMDA receptors. Sulphite is also directly toxic and can disrupt cerebral connective tissue and lens zonules, explaining the lens dislocation. The result is severe neuronal injury, cystic white matter change and progressive cerebral atrophy in the classic neonatal form.
additionalDifferentials: Molybdenum cofactor deficiency (biochemically similar but with low uric acid)
Neonatal epileptic encephalopathies of other causes
additionalInvestigations: Fresh urine sulphite testing and quantitation of urinary S-sulphocysteine
Plasma uric acid, which is normal (distinguishing it from molybdenum cofactor deficiency)
Plasma total homocysteine and cystine, which tend to be low
Neuroimaging showing early oedema followed by cystic change and atrophy
redFlags: Intractable neonatal seizures with rapidly evolving encephalopathy
Imaging suggesting hypoxic-ischaemic injury without a perinatal history
Ectopia lentis in an infant with neurological impairment
reference.prognosis: The classic neonatal form carries a poor prognosis, with severe neurodevelopmental impairment and often early death. Later-onset, attenuated forms follow a more variable course but still cause significant neurological disability; effective disease-modifying therapy is currently lacking.
pitfalls: Mistaking the presentation for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
Failing to distinguish it from molybdenum cofactor deficiency by not checking uric acid
Relying on stored urine for sulphite testing, as sulphite degrades quickly
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Attempt dietary restriction of the sulphur-containing amino acids methionine and cysteine as a substrate-reduction strategy, recognising its limited efficacy
Control intractable seizures with anticonvulsant therapy while avoiding agents that may worsen the metabolic state
Provide supportive nutrition via nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding and manage evolving spasticity with antispasticity agents and physiotherapy
Refer for ophthalmological assessment and management of ectopia lentis
Minimise catabolic stress from intercurrent illness and fasting
Coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic, neurology and palliative care given the severe neurodevelopmental impairment
Offer genetic counselling with carrier and prenatal testing for this autosomal recessive SUOX disorder
